issues.legal_issue: The civil court retains jurisdiction over an eviction suit after the statutory authority’s eviction power is removed, and a bar on challenging official orders does not itself bar that suit.
material_facts: The statutory power to decide eviction cases had been vested in a labour authority, but the provision conferring that power was deleted before the eviction suit was filed.
No replacement authority was given power to decide eviction cases after that deletion.
The suit sought eviction from accommodation and damages for its use and occupation; it did not seek to challenge an order made by the State or the labour authority.
issues.conclusion: The civil suit was within the civil court’s jurisdiction and was not barred by the statutory provision restricting challenges to official orders or actions.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, civil courts may try suits of a civil nature unless their jurisdiction is expressly or impliedly barred. The deletion of Section 21 of the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Housing Act removed the labour authority’s eviction jurisdiction without conferring it on another authority, restoring jurisdiction to the civil court. Section 13 of that Act restricts challenges to orders made by the State or labour authority and injunctions concerning actions under the Act; it does not oust jurisdiction over an employer’s eviction suit. Exclusion of civil jurisdiction is not readily inferred, must be explicit or clearly implied, and is construed strictly. No earlier judicial cases are cited.

rule.if: civil_eviction_suit and former_eviction_authority_power_removed and no_successor_eviction_forum_created and statutory_bar_limited_to_official_actions

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A claimant filed a civil suit seeking eviction from accommodation.
predicates.former_eviction_authority_power_removed: The law removed the specialized authority’s power to decide eviction cases.
predicates.no_successor_eviction_forum_created: The law did not give another specialized authority power to decide those eviction cases.
predicates.statutory_bar_limited_to_official_action: The statutory restriction concerned challenges to official orders or actions and did not cover the claimant’s eviction suit.

issues.definition: When a civil eviction suit is filed after the former eviction authority loses its power, no replacement forum is created, and the statutory bar is limited to challenges to official actions, the civil court can try the suit.

issues.legal_issue: An employer allotted industrial housing may sue to evict a worker when the State allotted the housing to the employer and the employer allotted it to the worker as part of the employment arrangement.
material_facts: The State allotted housing to the employer for allocation to its workers.
The employer allotted the quarter to a worker who was employed at its industrial unit and who applied for the quarter for his use and occupation.
The statutory scheme enabled the employer to deduct rent from the worker’s salary.
The employer filed the civil eviction suit against the worker’s successor in occupation.
issues.conclusion: The facts established a contractual relationship concerning the quarter, which could be treated as a tenancy agreement, and the employer was competent to sue for eviction.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the statutory scheme, including Section 20 of the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Housing Act, which enabled an employer to recover rent from an allottee-worker’s salary. The State’s allotment to the employer, the employer’s allotment to its employee, the rent-recovery arrangement, and the employment relationship together established a contractual relationship concerning the accommodation, construed as a tenancy agreement. No earlier judicial cases are cited.

rule.if: employer_eviction_suit and state_allotted_housing_to_employer and employer_allotted_housing_to_worker and worker_qualified_through_employment and rent_recovered_from_worker_salary

predicates.employer_eviction_suit: An employer filed a civil suit seeking eviction from accommodation it had provided to a worker.
predicates.state_allotted_housing_to_employer: The State allotted the accommodation to the employer for allocation to workers.
predicates.employer_allotted_housing_to_worker: The employer allotted the accommodation to the worker for the worker’s use and occupation.
predicates.worker_qualified_through_employment: The worker’s employment with the employer made the worker eligible for the accommodation.
predicates.rent_recovered_from_worker_salary: The arrangement allowed the employer to recover rent from the worker’s salary.

issues.definition: When an employer seeks eviction from State-allotted housing that it allocated to a worker because of the worker’s employment under an arrangement involving recovery of rent from salary, the employer can sue for eviction.

issues.legal_issue: A tenancy for accommodation provided as part of employment ends when the employment ends, and a worker’s family members who have no independent allotment have no right to remain in occupation.
material_facts: The worker received the quarter because he was employed by the employer.
The worker retired and received additional time to vacate, but did not vacate when that time expired.
The worker later died, and his wife and family continued to occupy the quarter.
The wife and other occupants were neither employed by the employer nor independently allotted the quarter.
issues.conclusion: The tenancy ended when the worker’s employment ended; the worker was obliged to surrender the quarter, and the family members had no independent right to remain. The Court upheld the eviction decree and the award of damages for use and occupation.
issues.legal_principle: A tenancy created between an employer and employee for accommodation connected with the employment lasts only for the period of employment and ends when the employment ends. The former employee must surrender the accommodation, and family members claiming through that employee cannot remain without an independent right to occupy it. The Court upheld the trial court’s eviction and damages findings on the facts. No earlier judicial cases are cited.

rule.if: civil_eviction_suit and service_linked_tenancy and employment_ended and occupant_or_successor_remained and successor_lacked_independent_allotment

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: An employer filed a civil suit seeking eviction from employment-related accommodation.
predicates.service_linked_tenancy: The worker occupied the accommodation under a tenancy connected with the worker’s employment.
predicates.employment_ended: The worker’s employment with the employer ended.
predicates.occupant_or_successor_remained: The worker or a person claiming through the worker continued to occupy the accommodation after the employment ended.
predicates.successor_lacked_independent_allotment: A person claiming through the worker had no separate allotment or other independent right to occupy the accommodation.

issues.definition: When an employer brings a civil eviction suit over employment-linked accommodation, the employment ends, and the worker or a successor without an independent allotment remains, the eviction and use-and-occupation damages may be upheld.

issues.legal_issue: The industrial housing regime does not prevent an employer company from using the statutory remedy available for company accommodation provided to an employee as part of employment.
material_facts: The employer was a company that had provided the quarter to a worker by virtue of his employment.
The worker retired without vacating the quarter, and his family continued in occupation after his death.
The employer’s suit was an eviction suit under the civil process; no complaint under the company-law remedy was before the Court.
issues.conclusion: The employer could also invoke the remedy available under Section 630 of the Companies Act, because the industrial housing regime did not bar that remedy.
issues.legal_principle: Section 630 of the Companies Act permits a company to complain when an employee fails to vacate company-provided accommodation on termination of employment, and provides for relief including recovery of the accommodation. The Court held that the industrial housing legislation did not bar resort to that remedy. This was an alternative remedy; the Court did not adjudicate a complaint under Section 630.

rule.if: company_housing_remedy_case and company_provided_housing_for_employment and employment_ended_without_vacation and no_statutory_bar_to_alternative_remedy

predicates.company_housing_remedy_case: A company seeks to use the statutory remedy concerning accommodation provided to an employee.
predicates.company_provided_housing_for_employment: The company provided accommodation to the employee because of the employment relationship.
predicates.employment_ended_without_vacation: The employee’s employment ended and the employee did not vacate the accommodation.
predicates.no_statutory_bar_to_alternative_remedy: The applicable housing regime did not prohibit the company from using the separate employee-housing remedy.

issues.definition: When a company seeks the employee-housing remedy for accommodation provided as part of employment, the employment has ended without the accommodation being vacated, and no law bars that alternative remedy, the company may invoke it.
